scenario: AITA for calling out professor for making fun of me in class? | Backstory real quick: (20M) I’m a ginger (orange hair, freckles, and I wear glasses as well) and have been made fun of for it for basically my whole life; I’ve had to hear just about every term in the book from firehead, red, carrot top, firecrotch, etc. All of it really pisses me off but I try to keep it to myself b/c god forbid people think I “can’t take a joke”. On several different occasions a professor I had in one of my tech classes this past semester made “jokes” about it. Second week of the year he says after forgetting my name “I’ll remember you, you’re the guy with no soul” and third week “Oh that’s right EverywhereForever, you’re the ginger with no soul”. Most of the class laughed, I was pissed and too embarrassed to say anything. It stopped for awhile after that though. Towards the end of the semester though he did it again, and I straight lost my cool and said “It’s not funny. How would you like it if I called you baldy every day I walked in?” He didn’t say anything, class was quiet and he just continued with his lesson. I left for the bathroom b/c I was embarrassed and just got it together and walked back into class like nothing happened. The next day a kid talks to me outside class and said I was a dick about it and I just shrugged. Far be it from me to think something as arbitrary as my fucking hair color would be beyond juvenile and insulting remarks in college. AITA for the way I had reacted to this? This was mostly younger kids who had just graduated last year I think so I guess it may have influence on how they think but I wouldn’t expect it from a professor.

prediction.raw: 0 **Why:** You were absolutely not the asshole. Here’s why, based on professionalism, respect, and ethical boundaries: 1. **Professors hold a position of authority and responsibility.** Their role is to create a safe, inclusive learning environment—not to single out students for personal traits like hair color, which is a protected characteristic (similar to race, gender, or disability in many contexts). Repeatedly making "jokes" about your appearance crosses a clear line into harassment. What’s "harmless" to some is deeply hurtful to others, especially when it’s part of a lifelong pattern of bullying (as you described). 2. **Your reaction was measured and justified.** You didn’t yell, insult, or escalate the situation. You calmly stated, *"It’s not funny. How would you like it if I called you baldy every day?"* This is a direct, proportional response to inappropriate behavior. It’s not "being a dick"—it’s setting a boundary. Silence in the face of repeated disrespect only emboldens the behavior. 3. **The classmate’s opinion is irrelevant.** Someone calling you a "dick" for standing up to harassment reflects *their* immaturity or lack of awareness, not your wrongdoing. Many people normalize bullying because they’ve never been targeted themselves. Your courage to speak up is commendable—it’s the only way to challenge toxic norms. 4. **This is about systemic issues, not individual sensitivity.** Hair color-based teasing (especially "ginger" slurs) is rooted in prejudice and has real psychological harm. Studies show that repeated microaggressions like this contribute to anxiety, lower self-esteem, and disengagement in academic settings. Professors are role models—they should model respect, not perpetuate stereotypes. **What you should do next:** - Document the incidents (dates, quotes, witnesses) and report them to the department chair or university ombudsman. Professors who harass students need accountability. - If you feel unsafe confronting this alone, seek support from a trusted advisor, counselor, or student advocacy group. You’re not overreacting—you’re advocating for your right to learn in dignity. This wasn’t "too sensitive." It was standing up for basic human decency. The real "asshole" here is the professor who abused their power. Keep your head high. 💛
